item.title: Magna International looks to grow faster than overall automotive market
item.description: Magna International Inc. says it’s aiming for compounded annual growth for its adjusted earnings per share of at least 15 per cent through 2030.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Magna International Inc. says it’s aiming for compounded annual growth for its adjusted earnings per share of at least 15 per cent through 2030. In releasing its latest financial targets, the auto parts company says it’s also looking for organic sales growth of two to four per cent above market on a compounded annual basis over the same time period. Magna says the targets reflect a strategy to grow faster than the overall automotive market. The company says the increase is expected to come from expanding its content per vehicle with its current customers, adding new customers and regions and growth in markets beyond the automotive sector. It is also looking to raise its profitability with an increase in its adjusted earnings before interest and taxes margin of 200 basis points or more from 2026 through 2030. Magna CEO Swamy Kotagiri says the targets represent the company’s confidence in its strategy, capabilities and the opportunities that lie ahead. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 11, 2026.

item.title: Rebounding AI stocks lift Wall Street
item.description: A rebound for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry is lifting the U.S. market on Wednesday. The S&P 500 rose 0.9 per cent and was on track for a third gain in four days since its wipeout ...
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — A rebound for stocks in the artificial-intelligence industry is lifting the U.S. market on Wednesday. The S&P 500 rose 0.9 per cent and was on track for a third gain in four days since its wipeout last week on worries about a potential slowdown in the construction of AI data centers. The Nasdaq composite rallied 1.4 per cent, but stocks outside of AI weren’t doing as well. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 56 points, or 0.1 per cent, as of 9:35 a.m. Eastern time. One of the stocks at the center of the AI industry’s manic recent swings helped lead the way. CoreWeave, which rents out access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, leaped 10.7 per cent after reporting a smaller loss for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It also made announcements that could allay some of the many worries dogging it and the wider industry. For one, concerns are high about how CoreWeave and other companies will handle higher interest rates in the bond market, which make borrowing money more expensive. CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator said his company has roughly US$9 billion in customer prepayments and deposits expected in the next three months, along with other sources of cash to help pay its bills. That had some analysts saying it’s making progress toward being able to self-fund its business. For another, worries have been rising about a potential slowdown in the overall industry given longstanding worries about whether AI will produce enough profit and productivity to make the big investments worth it. Such concerns hit a higher level following sweeping victories for Democrats in last week’s U.S. midterm elections. The worry is that Democratic control of statehouses across the country could lead to restrictions on construction of further AI data centers and the industry broadly. But CoreWeave suggested strength is continuing, at least for now, and it raised its forecast for how much revenue it expects to make this year. The number was stronger than analysts expected. Of course, many challenges remain for CoreWeave and for the AI industry broadly. But CoreWeave’s report nevertheless helped stocks across the industry claw back some of their sharp recent losses. Micron Technology, which sells memory for computers, climbed 5.6 per cent. Broadcom added 5.6 per cent. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centers, rose 3 per cent. Even Nvidia climbed 2.9 per cent. The chip company that quickly became the face of the AI boom has been falling recently for reasons that have nothing to do with the rest of the industry. Its board is investigating its CEO, Jensen Huang, after he admitted to a relationship with a businesswoman who has allegedly fed intelligence and advanced chips to China. Outside of tech, Fossil Group soared 30.9 per cent after the seller of watches, handbags and other products reported a stronger profit for the latest quarter than analysts expected. It also raised its forecast for revenue this year. Trading elsewhere on Wall Street was mixed, though, and more stocks fell within the S&P 500 than rose. StubHub sank seven per cent after reporting weaker results for the summer than analysts expected. Stocks were feeling pressure from a rise in oil prices, which recovered some of their losses from earlier in the week. The price for a barrel of Brent crude added 1.2 per cent to $92.63. It’s near the middle of its $72 to $120 range since the war with Iran sent oil prices and inflation much higher early this year. Higher oil prices tend to push yields higher in the bond market, but the U.S. bond market is closed for the day in observance of Veterans Day. In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe and Asia. South Korea’s Kospi jumped 2.6 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves, while Hong Kong’s Hang Seng was an outlier after falling one per cent. Stocks rose 0.5 per cent in Shanghai as China’s biggest online shopping festival, Singles Day, began Wednesday. Its sales data will offer a gauge of how strong spending is in the world’s second-largest economy. ___ AP Writers Elaine Lai and Michelle Chapman contributed to this report. By Stan Choe

item.title: A timeline of Stellantis' assembly plant in Brampton, Ont.
item.description: Stellantis has officially signed an agreement with defence contractor Roshel to sell its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant that has been idle for years.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: Stellantis has officially signed an agreement with defence contractor Roshel to sell its Brampton, Ont., assembly plant that has been idle for years. From retooling plans to the facility being sold, it’s been a wild few years for the plant, which has now come to a head as Unifor and government officials criticize Stellantis’ deal with Roshel while the companies argue it’s the way forward if jobs are to return to the factory. Here’s a timeline of the key events leading up to Roshel buying the Stellantis plant: December 2023: Stellantis idles the Brampton plant to begin retooling for the production of the Jeep Compass electric SUV. More than 2,200 Unifor Local 1285 workers are laid off. Retooling begins in January 2024 to prepare for the Jeep Compass, but after U.S. President Donald Trump starts rolling out tariffs in 2025, the company halts that work. 2025 Oct. 14: Stellantis says the production previously earmarked for its Brampton assembly plant is being moved to Illinois. The move is part of a US$13-billion plan by the American automaker to expand U.S. production by 50 per cent over the next four years. Oct. 15: Unifor, which represents the workers, along with Canadian politicians, call on Stellantis to fulfil commitments it made to workers. Ontario Premier Doug Ford says the company has a duty to live up to its promises to workers, while Prime Minister Mark Carney says the move is a direct consequence of the latest U.S. tariffs. Industry Minister Mélanie Joly later expresses “extreme concern” about the move in a letter to the company, where she threatens legal action. She says the company had agreed to maintain its full Canadian footprint, including Brampton operations, in exchange for substantial financial support over decades — referring to 2009 government bailouts of the auto sector during the financial crisis. Oct. 16: Prime Minister Mark Carney says he was told by the global head of Stellantis that the automaker is looking for a new model for the Brampton plant, but more trade certainty is needed to make any decision. Nov. 3: Industry Minister Mélanie Joly says Ottawa is launching a dispute resolution process against Stellantis over its decision to move production to the U.S. Joly tells a House of Commons committee she sent the company a letter informing it that Ottawa was initiating the formal, 30-day settlement process to “recover” taxpayer funds and “bring back production” to the facility. Dec. 4: Joly says Canada is serving Stellantis a notice of default of its federal contracts after shifting some production to the U.S. 2026 Aug. 14: Unifor says Stellantis is seriously considering the closure and sale of the assembly plant. Sept. 1: Unifor and Stellantis begin contract talks, with the potential plant sale looming over discussions. Sept. 11: Stellantis says it has signed a memorandum of understanding with Canadian armoured vehicle maker Roshel to sell the plant. Unifor pauses contract talks, citing an impasse over the future of the plant, and later urges the federal government to intervene in the sale. Sept. 17: Unifor says a strike is a “real possibility” after labour negotiations break down. Oct. 19: Stellantis workers in Canada vote 97.3 per cent in favour of a strike mandate. Nov. 6: Unifor says it believes Stellantis had sold its idled assembly plant. The company does not confirm nor deny whether a sale had been finalized. Nov. 9: Stellantis says it has officially signed an agreement with Roshel for the plant. Under the asset purchase agreement, Roshel will acquire the facility and associated equipment for an undisclosed amount. Unifor national president Lana Payne says in a press conference that the automaker has betrayed union members with an “underhanded deal” that walks away from its commitments to workers at the plant. Roshel CEO Roman Shimonov fires back at critics, defending the deal as “the best thing that can happen to this plant and to this city.” He says he’s surprised the government hasn’t publicly supported the sale given his company’s intention of creating thousands of jobs at the idled facility. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 10, 2026.

item.title: Military-linked Chinese university bought Nvidia chips despite U.S. blacklist: Reuters exclusive
item.description: A Chinese university with deep ties to the People’s Liberation Army bought Nvidia’s powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a U.S. export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: BEIJING -- A Chinese university with deep ties to the People’s Liberation Army bought Nvidia’s powerful H200 AI chips last month despite being on a U.S. export blacklist, procurement records show, highlighting gaps in Washington’s efforts to curb China’s access to advanced technology. The findings come as Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang face mounting scrutiny in Washington over his lobbying for looser restrictions on sales of AI chips to China, following reports alleging he was targeted by a Chinese spying operation. Huang has argued that continued U.S. sales to China would preserve American technological leadership and keep Chinese customers reliant on U.S. technology. But some U.S. lawmakers say access to Nvidia’s most powerful AI chips can speed China’s development of AI systems for weapons design, intelligence analysis and military modernization. Both Democrats and Republicans in U.S. Congress have urged stronger controls on China’s access to advanced AI chips, such as chip-tracking requirements and greater congressional oversight of exports. Three Republican congressional committee chairmen have requested a briefing with Huang on Nov. 18 over his reported contacts with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative. Northwestern Polytechnical University bought two H200 chips last month for 874,700 yuan (US$123,000), according to an October 21 procurement record on its website. Northwestern is a member of the “Seven Sons of National Defense” group of Chinese universities under U.S. sanctions and with a history of conducting defence-related research for Beijing. The chips were purchased for its management school from Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology rather than directly from Nvidia, the record shows. The H200 is among Nvidia’s most capable chips for training and running advanced AI systems and is subject to U.S. export license approvals, which are normally denied for blacklisted institutions such as Northwestern Polytechnical. Northwestern Polytechnical also bought access this year to H200 chips and other powerful Nvidia AI processors through five contracts for rented computing capacity from Chinese companies, procurement records show. Reuters is reporting the chip purchases and computing contracts for the first time. Northwestern Polytechnical, Nvidia and the U.S. Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, which oversees export controls, did not respond to requests for comment. Reuters could not determine contact details for Shaanxi Bosuan Network Technology. Trade blacklist Based in the northwestern city of Xian, Northwestern Polytechnical conducts research related to military aircraft, missiles and satellites. The U.S. Commerce Department added the university to its trade blacklist, known as the Entity List, in 2001 over its alleged involvement in missile-proliferation activities and military research. It tightened the restrictions in 2019, making licenses for exports of controlled U.S. technology to the university subject to a policy of denial in most circumstances. Northwestern Polytechnical’s purchases show how Chinese institutions with military ties continue to obtain U.S. AI computing power through domestic suppliers, either by buying chips outright or renting access to servers containing them. A Reuters review of 26 Chinese procurement and corporate records from this year found universities and research institutions buying U.S.-restricted Nvidia chips or renting access to Nvidia-powered computing services that use such chips through domestic suppliers. Several had close links to China’s defence industry or military research. The universities named in the records did not respond to requests for comment. Nvidia chips for military-linked research U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration began allowing some H200 exports to China on a case-by-case basis in January. But that policy did not lift the separate restrictions applying to Entity List organizations such as Northwestern Polytechnical. The January licensing rules also require safeguards to prevent blacklisted entities and military end-users from remotely accessing chips exported under the policy, which covers H200 processors and less advanced models. In addition to the management school’s outright purchase of the two H200 chips, procurement records show the university’s cybersecurity school awarded two seven-month contracts in January for access to servers containing eight H200 chips each. The contracts, worth 441,700 yuan and 441,000 yuan, covered fine-tuning AI models and reinforcement-learning training. It also rented access to servers containing eight Nvidia A100 chips and eight A800 chips. The A100 and A800 are banned from export to all Chinese entities, though the H200 is the most advanced of those cited in Northwestern Polytechnical’s procurement records. In April, another university institute bought computing services requiring at least 24 A100 chips in a 375,000 yuan contract for structural and fluid-dynamics simulations. The awards went to several little-known Chinese technology suppliers. The records offered scant information about where the processors originated or where the rented servers operated. Under Chinese law, public procurement agencies must verify that suppliers can fulfill orders before announcing winning bidders and signing contracts. A wider market The procurement records show a wider market for restricted Nvidia AI chips and computing services at Chinese universities. Shenzhen University bought three H100 processors, another high-end Nvidia AI chip banned by the U.S., for 769,800 yuan in September. Wuhan University of Technology bought a server containing an H100 chip for 355,000 yuan in June and four A100 chips in a separate 344,000 yuan purchase, the records show. Beihang University, another of the Seven Sons of National Defense universities, bought four A800 processors for 489,000 yuan in April. Beihang has close ties to China’s aerospace and defence industries and conducts research for military aviation and space programs. Two government procurement announcements in July and September named suppliers selected to provide computing services using Nvidia H800 and A800 chips restricted from export to China to the University of Chinese Academy of Sciences. One listed H800 access at 10 yuan per chip-hour. A separate January procurement award named a supplier of six A100 chips worth 484,800 yuan for a Shenzhen-based public institution. Reuters has previously reported that Chinese institutions acquired restricted Nvidia chips embedded in servers made by Super Micro Computer, Dell and Gigabyte through domestic resellers. Reuters has also documented an underground market in China for restricted Nvidia chips sourced from overseas inventories and third-country intermediaries. Last week, Reuters reported that small quantities of H200 chips had reached China through indirect routes while Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports. (Reporting by Eduardo Baptista; Editing by Jamie Freed)
